verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2505.18949v1 (Yun, An, Wang, Peng, Shang; UCSD). Table 5, Semantic Diversity block, WritingPrompts row, columns Full Template / Simple Steer / Full Template w/ Diversity = 0.3291 / 0.4767 / 0.3427, exactly as claimed (Llama-3b model). Claim carries no quote; all three figures and their column assignment appear verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids model collapse.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2404.01413v2, Abstract: 'then demonstrate that accumulating the successive generations of synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids model collapse; these results hold across a range of model sizes, architectures, and hyperparameters.' Quote fragment matches word for word across the PDF line break; Gerstgrasser/Schaeffer/Dey/Rafailov (Stanford et al.) confirmed on page 1.

verdicts.trueWording: Replacing real data by each generation's synthetic data does tend toward collapse.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2404.01413v2, Abstract: 'We confirm that replacing the original real data by each generation's synthetic data does indeed tend towards model collapse'. Quote fragment verbatim; the claim's 'confirm' matches the paper's own verb.

verdicts.trueWording: Aligned models generally display less diversity than instruction fine-tuned counterparts.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2411.04427 (Murthy, Ullman, Hu; Harvard/Kempner), Abstract: 'While no model reaches human-like diversity, aligned models generally display less diversity than their instruction fine-tuned counterparts.' Quote verbatim across the hyphenated line break. The 'conceptual' qualifier the claim adds is the paper's own framing (title: 'Alignment reduces language models' conceptual diversity'; Introduction: 'aligned models generally display less conceptual diversity than their non-aligned, fine-tuned counterparts').

verdicts.trueWording: While no model reaches human-like diversity.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2411.04427, Abstract: 'While no model reaches human-like diversity...'. Quote verbatim. The 'conceptual' limb is carried by the Introduction ('no model approaches human-like conceptual diversity') and the Conclusion ('no model reached human-level conceptual diversity').

verdicts.trueWording: Preference-tuned models exhibit greater effective semantic diversity than SFT or base.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2504.12522 (COLM 2025; Shypula, Li, Zhang, Padmakumar, Yin, Bastani), Section 1: 'in both code generation and creative writing, we find that preference-tuned models exhibit greater effective semantic diversity.' Abstract adds the comparison class: 'these same preference-tuned models generate greater effective semantic diversity than SFT or base models.' The claim's 'once quality thresholds are applied' is the paper's own definition of effective semantic diversity ('diversity among outputs that meet quality thresholds').

verdicts.trueWording: Code generation only: within high-quality outputs, preference-tuned models less diverse.
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in Section 1 of arXiv:2504.12522: 'A deeper analysis in code generation shows that when restricting to high-quality generations only, preference-tuned models produce less semantically diverse content within that subset.' But the claim drops the paper's explicit domain restriction. Section 5 confirms the scope: the restricted analysis is run 'to those in Table 2 for code, but restrict the analysis to only valid generations'; no equivalent within-quality finding is reported for creative writing. The paper also immediately counterweights it: 'preference tuning increases the proportion of high-quality outputs to such an extent that this gain outweighs the reduction in diversity per high-quality sample.'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the unrestricted scope - the paper confines this finding to code generation, not generation at large

verdicts.trueWording: For open-ended creative writing, preference tuning links to greater lexical diversity.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2504.12522, Section 1: 'For open-ended creative writing, preference tuning is linked to greater diversity in lexical patterns.' Quote verbatim, whole sentence, including the creative-writing scope the claim preserves.

verdicts.trueWording: Trained models had higher diversity than diversity-prompted GPT-4o-iter.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2503.17126 (Chung, Padmakumar, Roemmele, Sun, Kreminski; Midjourney/NYU), Section 5.2 Results: 'our trained models had higher diversity than existing models (even higher than *GPT-4o-iter, which used diversity-inducing prompts)'. Quote verbatim including the bullet marker before GPT-4o-iter.

verdicts.trueWording: Gold scored lower reward than those models but diversity was far higher.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2503.17126, Section 5.2: 'Human-crafted *Gold showed a lower reward score than these models but the diversity was far higher.' 'These models' is the preceding sentence's cluster of instruction-tuned models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-iter, o1, Claude-3.5-sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, Instruct), and the reward is reddit-reward, a reward model the authors trained themselves (Section 4: 'we trained a reward model out of (x, y, s) triplets in the dataset'). Every limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Best 8B model achieved on-par diversity as a human-created dataset.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2503.17126, Abstract: 'Our best model with 8B parameters could achieve on-par diversity as a human-created dataset while having output quality similar to the best instruction-tuned models we examined, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1.' Quote verbatim. The 'deviation-weighted objective' limb is the paper's method: 'we weighted the pair's training objective with the deviation of the winning [instances]' (DDPO/DORPO), and Section 5.2 names the Llama-3.1-8B DDPO-both model as the best on both axes.

verdicts.trueWording: KL-based regularization bias could in extreme cases cause preference collapse.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2405.16455v2, Abstract: 'suffers from an inherent algorithmic bias due to its Kullback-Leibler-based regularization in optimization. In extreme cases, this bias could lead to a phenomenon we term preference collapse, where minority preferences are virtually disregarded.' Quote verbatim. Page 1 confirms JASA acceptance. Note the paper hedges with 'could lead to' where the claim says 'produces', but the claim retains 'in extreme cases', so the conditionality survives.

verdicts.trueWording: 29% to 41% improvement in alignment, by one metric, over standard RLHF.
verdicts.note: Raw PDF text of arXiv:2405.16455v2, Abstract: 'demonstrating a 29% to 41% improvement in alignment with human preferences, as measured by a certain metric, compared to standard RLHF.' Claim carries no quote; both figures appear verbatim. Introduction supplies the metric and mechanism: preference matching divergence falls from 2.23 to 1.57 (Llama-2-7B) and 1.16 to 0.68 (OPT-1.3B), 'marking improvements of approximately 29% and 41%, respectively' - so the claim's 'on one metric' is exact.

verdicts.trueWording: Multiple credible sources: text-davinci-002 was not trained with RLHF.
verdicts.note: lesswrong.com returned HTTP 429 to a browser user agent, so the page was reached by two further routes: the Wayback raw capture of the exact URL (web.archive.org/web/20260725093614id_/...) and the AI Alignment Forum copy of the same post (8th Nov 2022), cross-checked against greaterwrong.com. All three carry the 'Important correction' section at the head of the post, verbatim: 'I have received evidence from multiple credible sources that text-davinci-002 was not trained with RLHF.' The correction limb is fully supported (the title was formerly 'Mysteries of mode collapse due to RLHF'). What the page does not support is the coinage limb: nowhere does it claim janus coined the mode-collapse usage, and the post itself has a section 'Examples of mode collapse from prior work' describing cases 'found by other people', which cuts against it.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that janus coined the mode-collapse usage - the page never says so, and its own prior-work section points the other way

verdicts.trueWording: Higher temperature flattens the distribution into undifferentiated goo first.
verdicts.note: Same three routes as index 796 (Wayback raw capture of the lesswrong URL, Alignment Forum copy, greaterwrong mirror), section 'Why not just turn up the temperature?': 'Increasing the sampling temperature will flatten the rest of the output distribution into undifferentiated goo before it begins to be helpful for escaping from the high confidence attractor.' Quote verbatim; every limb of the claim is in that one sentence.
